findings.text: A newcomer learns what Athena is in the first two sentences, before anything else on the page. That covers the 'what is it' question.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says why it exists: it shows that Athena can explain a project with every statement traced to source lines. It never connects this to the first sentence, though. A newcomer told that Athena 'turns a short request into a change to a code repository' cannot tell how a study fits that job, or whether studies are a main feature or a side demo.
findings.source: header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: The next step is easy to find: it is linked from the top and has its own section. That section only points to the GitHub repository, with no install command, so a newcomer who wants to try Athena must leave the page with no sense of the effort involved.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself"; section "Next steps"

findings.text: Before the page says what firstmate is, it defines seven firstmate-specific terms. Several of them use words not yet explained, such as 'secondmate', 'merge authority' and 'guarded fast-forward'. A newcomer meets jargon before the basic picture, which is the reverse of what helps.
findings.source: Heading "Start here" > "Words used first" (captain, yolo, in scope, green, red, local-only landing, home)

findings.text: The definition of 'home' introduces 'secondmate' without explaining it. This shows that even the 'Start here' layer leans on terms a stranger lacks.
findings.source: "home: A firstmate home is the place that holds a backlog of tasks. A secondmate is a persistent home of its own, not a task in someone else's backlog."

findings.text: Once reached, the description of firstmate is clear and concrete. The numbered walk-through 'One piece of work, start to finish' gives a usable step-by-step picture.
findings.source: Heading "What firstmate is": "Firstmate is a tool for people who direct AI coding agents. It keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a worker..."

findings.text: This section uses transition ids before the Transitions section defines them, so a top-to-bottom reader cannot follow the reference.
findings.source: Heading "Counters": "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The findings jump from f1 to f3 with no f2, and nothing explains the gap. A careful newcomer may think something was left out.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": items f1, f3, f4

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to exact lines at a pinned commit. This shows the traceability that the lede promises.
findings.source: Heading "Claims and sources" and the bracketed ids such as "[c11]" throughout

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine analysis of firstmate. A newcomer who came to the Athena site to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on Athena and many screens on another tool. The page serves as a sample of Athena's output, not as an introduction to Athena.
findings.source: Overall page structure: headings States, Counters, Transitions, Why it is built this way, Glossary, 44 claims
